docs.lumenfield:
Lumenfield (fictional) Quarterly Business Review, Q3. Prepared by the leadership team for the all-hands on 14 October. This document summarises how the quarter went, what we learned from customers, and the priorities for the next two quarters. It is intended for everyone at the company, so it explains terms where it can, but readers are expected to be familiar with the product.

About the company. Lumenfield makes scheduling software for small and medium-sized clinics: dentists, physiotherapists, veterinary practices and private GP surgeries. A practice uses our product to let patients book online, to send reminders by text message, and to fill gaps in the diary when someone cancels. We have 212 employees across offices in Leeds, Lisbon and Toronto, and our customers span nine countries.

How the teams are organised. Product and Engineering are split into four squads: Booking, Reminders, Billing and Platform. Each squad has a product manager, a designer and between four and seven engineers. Customer Success is organised by region, and the Sales team is split between inbound practices and a smaller group that works with larger clinic groups. People Operations and Finance report to the chief operating officer.

People and culture. Hiring continued across all squads, with a focus on engineers who have worked in regulated industries. The average time to fill a role was 38 days. Employee survey results were positive overall: 86 percent of staff said they would recommend Lumenfield as a place to work, though several teams reported that meetings had become too frequent. A review of meeting habits is planned for the autumn, led by People Operations.

Customer stories. A physiotherapy group in Manchester reduced missed appointments by a third after switching on text reminders. A veterinary practice in Lisbon told us the waiting list feature saved the front desk about five hours a week. A dental clinic in Toronto, our first customer in Canada, praised the quality of onboarding. These stories are used by Marketing and are shared with the product squads each month.

Support operations. The support team handled 31,000 conversations in the quarter, with a median first reply time of eleven minutes. Most questions were about changing reminder wording, importing existing diaries and setting up staff rotas. A new help centre launched in August, and we expect it to deflect around one in five questions by the end of the year. Weekend cover now rotates between the three regional teams.

Product roadmap, in brief. After the integration marketplace, the Reminders squad will explore voice call reminders for patients who do not use text messages. Billing will add support for split payments between insurers and patients. Platform will finish moving the oldest services to the new framework, which should halve the time needed for a routine release. Dates for all of these are provisional and depend on hiring.

Highlights of the quarter. The new waiting-list feature shipped in July and was switched on for every customer by the end of August. The mobile booking page was rebuilt and is now twice as fast to load. We opened the Toronto office, hired eleven people there, and ran our first customer conference with 180 attendees. Support satisfaction stayed above 94 percent throughout the quarter.

Retention. The number leadership watches most closely is the monthly churn rate, the percentage of paying customers who cancel in a given month. It rose from 1.8 percent to 2.4 percent after the price change in June, and the target for the end of the year is to bring the churn rate back under 2 percent. Exit interviews show that small single-site practices are most sensitive to price, while multi-site groups mostly leave because of missing integrations.

Growth. Annual recurring revenue (ARR) closed the quarter at 14.2 million, up from 12.9 million at the start of the year. Net revenue retention (NRR) was 108 percent, because customers who stayed upgraded to higher plans and added extra locations. Gross margin was 78 percent. The cost of winning a new customer, measured as CAC payback, was 14 months, which is within our target of 18.

Security and compliance. Larger customers now ask for evidence before they sign. The Henley Health group, which would be our biggest customer to date, will not sign its contract until we provide our SOC 2 report. The auditors are due on site in March, and the security team has been collecting evidence since August. We also hold ISO 27001 certification, and we are updating our data processing agreements for the new privacy rules in Canada.

Risks. The main risks are the pace of hiring in Toronto, a dependence on one text message provider for reminders, and the possibility that the price change keeps pushing small practices away. Mitigations are being tracked by the risk committee, which meets monthly. Finance also flagged that foreign exchange movements could cost up to 0.4 million next year.

Priorities for Q4 and Q1. First, bring churn back under target by improving onboarding for single-site practices. Second, complete the audit and sign Henley Health. Third, launch the integration marketplace so multi-site groups can connect their existing systems. Fourth, hire a head of customer education. Each priority has an owner who will report progress at the monthly review.

Questions and feedback. Please send questions to the leadership mailbox or raise them at the all-hands. Teams can request a deeper walkthrough of any section from Finance or from the strategy team. The next review will be held in January.
docs.harbourview:
Harbourview Logistics (fictional) Year-End Finance Review. Prepared by the finance team for the board meeting on 9 December. The document covers results for the year, the position at the balance sheet date, and the main accounting judgements made in preparing the figures. It is written for directors who are not accountants, though some technical terms are unavoidable.

About the company. Harbourview moves goods for retailers and manufacturers across the United Kingdom and Ireland. We run 38 depots, a fleet of 410 vehicles and two large automated sorting hubs. We employ 2,900 people, most of them drivers and warehouse staff. About two thirds of our revenue comes from contracts with the ten largest customers, which is why customer concentration appears every year in our risk register.

The year in brief. Volumes grew by 6 percent, helped by a new contract with a national grocery chain from March. Fuel costs fell in the second half, and driver turnover improved after the pay review in April. The new routing platform went live in January and has reduced empty running by nine percent. Two depots were closed and one new depot opened in the Midlands.

Our people. Average headcount rose by 140, mostly drivers and warehouse operatives. We trained 310 drivers for the new low-emission vehicles and opened a second apprenticeship scheme with two regional colleges. Accident rates fell for the third year running. Sickness absence was 4.1 percent, slightly above our target, and the people team is working with depot managers on rota design and support for returning staff.

Customers and contracts. Eleven contracts came up for renewal during the year and ten were renewed, most on improved terms. The one loss was a regional furniture retailer that moved to an in-house fleet. We won six new customers, including the grocery chain, a pharmaceutical wholesaler and two online retailers. Service levels were met in 97 percent of deliveries, against a target of 96.

Sustainability. Emissions per delivered parcel fell by eight percent, driven by fuller loads, electric vans in three city depots and the shift to cleaner fuel for long-distance routes. We have committed to science-based targets and will report progress in the annual report. Two depots now generate part of their own electricity from rooftop solar panels, and a third installation is planned for next year.

Risk register. The principal risks remain customer concentration, driver availability, fuel price volatility and cyber security. The audit committee reviewed each risk in detail during the year. A tabletop exercise on a ransomware scenario in September led to changes in backup procedures and in how depots communicate when systems are unavailable. The register is updated every quarter.

Capital investment. The routing platform was capitalised at 2.5 million, covering licences, configuration and internal development time. Its cost is written off through amortisation over five years, starting in January, so each year carries an amortisation charge of 0.5 million. Vehicles and sorting equipment continue to be depreciated over their useful lives, and no change has been made to those policies.

Profit measures. The board has asked to focus on EBITDA, earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, rather than net profit, because the depreciation charge and the one-off cost of closing two depots distort the year-on-year picture. EBITDA for the year was 41.3 million, compared with 37.8 million last year. Net profit was lower because of higher interest on the new vehicle lease.

Cash. Working capital is tight, because several large customers pay on 90-day terms while we pay fuel and wages immediately. The finance team has negotiated a short-term facility to cover the gap and is working with the largest customers to move to 60-day terms. Cash at the year end was 18.6 million, within the covenant limits set by our lenders.

Revenue recognition. Annual contracts with retailers are invoiced up front. Cash received for periods that have not yet been served is not counted as income straight away; it sits on the balance sheet as deferred revenue and is released month by month as the service is delivered. At the year end deferred revenue stood at 7.9 million, up from 6.4 million, reflecting the new grocery contract.

Judgements and estimates. The main estimates in the accounts relate to the useful life of the routing platform, the provision for disputed delivery claims, and the fair value of fuel hedges. The auditors have reviewed each of these and have not raised any adjustments. A full list of accounting policies is available from the finance team on request.

Outlook. Next year's budget assumes volume growth of 4 percent, stable fuel prices and a further reduction in empty running. Capital spending will fall to 22 million. The board is asked to approve the budget, the dividend proposal and the refinancing timetable at the meeting.
docs.kestrel:
Project Kestrel (fictional) Migration Plan, version 3. Owned by the platform engineering team, reviewed by the architecture group and the head of operations. This document describes how the booking service will move from our old data centre to the new cloud platform, who does what, and how we will know whether the move has gone well. It is meant to be read by engineers, support staff and managers.

Background. The booking service handles every reservation made through our apps and partner sites. It currently runs on servers in a rented data centre, on hardware that is nearly six years old. Capacity is limited, upgrades take weeks, and the lease ends in September. Moving to the cloud platform lets us add capacity in minutes and gives us better monitoring and automatic backups.

Scope. The migration covers the booking API, the pricing engine, the notification worker and the main database. It does not cover the reporting warehouse or the internal admin tools, which will move later in the year. The mobile apps and partner integrations do not change; they keep using the same addresses and the same authentication.

Team and responsibilities. Platform engineering has nine engineers, split between infrastructure and tooling. The booking squad has six engineers who know the service best and will be involved throughout. Operations provides two on-call engineers each shift, and the security team reviews the configuration before every major step. A rota for the cutover weekend is published two weeks in advance.

Testing strategy. Besides unit tests, each stage includes load tests at twice the busiest hour we have ever seen, tests with deliberately broken dependencies, and a full rehearsal of the weekend with the actual runbooks. Test results are recorded in the shared tracker, and any failed check must be explained and closed before the next stage starts. Support staff test the admin tools against the new environment.

Data. The main database holds eleven years of bookings, about 1.4 terabytes. We will copy it continuously while the old system is live and verify counts, checksums and a sample of records. Personal data stays within the same regions as before. After the migration, backups are taken every hour and kept for thirty days, and restore tests happen monthly.

Security. The new environment follows the company baseline: encrypted storage, restricted network access, short-lived credentials for engineers and automatic scanning of dependencies. Penetration testing is scheduled for April by an outside firm. Any high-severity finding must be fixed before the cutover, and medium findings are reviewed by the architecture group.

Timeline. Environment design finishes in March. Load testing runs through April. The cutover is scheduled for the second weekend of May, starting at 22:00 on Saturday, because bookings are lowest then. After the cutover there is a two-week monitoring period before the old servers are switched off. Support will have extra staff on call for the first week.

Availability target. Throughout the cutover and the weeks after it we commit to an uptime SLA of 99.9 percent for the booking API, which allows roughly 43 minutes of downtime in a month. Any breach must be reported to the head of operations within an hour and reviewed in a written post-incident note.

Cutover approach. We will use a blue-green deployment. The new environment, called green, is built next to the live one, called blue, and is tested with copies of real traffic. When the checks pass, traffic is switched from blue to green in a single step by changing the load balancer. Blue is kept running and untouched so that nothing has to be rebuilt if we need to go back.

Controlled release. Work that is not fully ready by the weekend will not block the migration. It ships switched off behind a feature flag, a setting that can be turned on for a small group of users first, then for everyone, without a new release. The flags are owned by the squad that wrote the feature, and each flag has an expiry date after which it must be removed.

What happens if it goes wrong. During the first hour after the switch the on-call engineer watches the error rate and response times. If errors rise above 2 percent, or the booking API is unavailable for more than five minutes, the engineer follows the rollback plan: traffic is switched back to blue, the database changes are reversed using the prepared scripts, and the incident manager is notified. The plan has been rehearsed twice in the test environment.

Roles. The migration lead coordinates the weekend and makes the go or no-go decision. The database owner is responsible for data copying and verification. The incident manager runs communications. Support leads handle customer questions, and the head of operations signs off the final result on Monday morning.

Communication. Partners are told two weeks in advance, customers see a notice in the apps the day before, and the status page is updated at every stage. After the migration a short review will be held to record what worked and what should change for the next move.
